title: Epoch distribution and class balance
question: How do serial position, sequence length and trial outcome shape the data available for each relative class?
summary: Later classes contribute fewer clean epochs and a smaller share from successful trials, especially in the older-adult cohort.
motivation: The capacity-normalized labels change with serial position and individual span. To understand what drives the comparisons, both cohorts were audited for differences in sample composition across the four classes.
methods: Cross-tabulate retained clean encoding epochs from both successful and unsuccessful trials by cohort, relative class, absolute sequence length L, serial position k, and outcome. Count items above individual span separately as unclassified where applicable. Compute the percentage of clean epochs in each class that come from successfully completed trials. Participant-level workbooks retain the underlying stratification.
results: In the older-adult cohort, C2 contributed 10,304 clean epochs and C4 contributed 2,795. In the young-adult cohort, the corresponding counts were 1,014 and 438. From C1 to C4, the share of clean epochs from successful trials fell from 70.78% to 24.97% in the older-adult cohort and from 84.77% to 68.72% in the young-adult cohort. The heatmaps show that a fixed serial position can appear in multiple classes because spans differ.
interpretation: These are differences in epoch availability and outcome composition. The sampling pattern follows from the task rules, individual span and artifact rejection. The high-class imbalance motivates both participant-level pairing and a separate successful-trial restriction.
conclusion: Data availability varies substantially by class. The estimates in the later classes rest on fewer epochs, and restricting connectivity inference to successful trials addresses a marked outcome imbalance.
limitations: Epoch-based percentages describe the composition of retained epochs. Trial-level success is tabulated separately in the manuscript. Equal contribution to paired inference leaves unequal precision in the underlying participant estimates.
keywords: imbalance distribution outcome counts heatmap capacity L k

title: Connectivity during successful trials
question: Do the class-dependent connectivity results persist when every included trial ends in correct recall?
summary: Shannon complexity differences persisted after restricting the analysis to clean epochs from successful trials in both cohorts.
motivation: A greater fraction of high-class epochs came from unsuccessfully completed trials. Incorrect recall could be associated with attention lapses or other differences in behavior, making it important to examine the connectivity patterns within successful trials.
methods: Restrict the analysis to clean encoding epochs from trials in which the full sequence was reproduced correctly. Compare paired participant-level measures by relative class using the same class rule, bands and regions. The revised main figures use this subset, with a family of 300 Benjamini–Hochberg-adjusted tests per cohort.
results: In the older-adult cohort, all Shannon complexity class pairs differed after correction across all five bands and both regions. In the young-adult cohort, differences were present across bands and regions, with some contrasts remaining inconclusive. The authors report more significant contrasts following the restriction than in the earlier mixed-outcome analysis.
interpretation: Connectivity differences remain when unsuccessful trials are excluded. The result reduces the plausibility of an explanation based solely on the inclusion of unsuccessful trials. Relative class can still reflect serial position and other correlated aspects of task performance.
conclusion: The successful-trial analysis supports an association with relative progression during correct sequence encoding. The revised main results use this analysis.
limitations: The earlier mixed-outcome statistical matrices are unavailable in the current repository. The design does not establish the presence of cognitive overload, and restriction to successful trials conditions on performance.
manuscript: Methods II.B, Results III and Figs. 3–6
keywords: outcome success Wilcoxon failed correct recall Shannon

title: Sequence length at fixed serial position
question: At the same serial position and relative class, does absolute sequence length affect Shannon graph complexity?
summary: No sequence-length contrasts survived FDR correction in the older-adult cohort.
motivation: Serial position progresses within a sequence and longer sequences are usually encountered later in the task. Comparing lengths at fixed position and relative class probes whether absolute task length or across-task progression alone accounts for the reported pattern.
methods: In the older-adult cohort, compare available sequence lengths L within each fixed absolute position k and relative class. Plot mean participant Shannon complexity from clean encoding epochs in frontal and parietal regions for each band. Use paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests and one Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction across this analysis.
results: Across theta, alpha, low beta, high beta and gamma, Shannon complexity was generally similar across the available lengths within a given position and class. No pairwise contrast remained statistically significant after correction. Longer lengths offered fewer observations and some strata showed more variable distributions.
interpretation: The analysis found no detectable systematic sequence-length effect in comparable strata of the older-adult cohort. This weakens a simple absolute-length account of the main pattern. Sparse data can still conceal meaningful effects.
conclusion: Absolute sequence length alone did not account for the observed class pattern within the comparisons available.
limitations: This control was confined to one cohort and did not fully separate relative class from absolute serial position. Within-sequence fatigue, attention and other order effects remain plausible. The null result does not establish equivalence.
keywords: sequence length serial position fatigue task progression confounding L k

title: Strength, path length and clustering
question: How do other weighted graph measures describe the class-dependent network patterns?
summary: The class contrasts for strength, path length and clustering vary by cohort, frequency band and region.
motivation: Changes in Shannon complexity combine entropy and dispersion. Complementary descriptors help identify which properties of weighted networks vary alongside the main result.
methods: Characterize sensor networks from pairwise orthogonalized amplitude envelope correlation (AEC). Assess node strength, characteristic path length and weighted clustering across C1–C4 in five bands and two regions, separately by cohort. Use clean epochs from successfully completed trials and paired participant-level inference in the main analysis.
results: In the older-adult cohort, high-beta path length differed between C4 and each lower class in both regions (adjusted p < 0.01, S3). In the young-adult cohort, the clearest strength and clustering differences involving C4 were in the gamma band (S2 and S6). Path-length contrasts in the young-adult cohort showed limited evidence of class separation (S4).
interpretation: The paired contrasts are specific to each measure, band and region. Parietal node strength was descriptively higher than frontal node strength in the young-adult cohort across bands and classes (S2). Regional strength can depend on electrode coverage and other acquisition differences.
conclusion: The extra metrics identify band- and region-specific differences that complement the broader Shannon complexity pattern.
limitations: The matrices show within-cohort contrasts with rounded p and r values. Differences between cohort profiles cannot be attributed to age because the protocols, sensors and samples differ.
manuscript: Methods II.E, Results III, Table III and Figs. 5–6
keywords: node strength characteristic path length weighted clustering shortest path older-adult cohort young-adult cohort

title: Weighted community organization
question: Does weighted modularity provide complementary evidence about community organization across relative classes?
summary: Modularity varied across multiple bands and both regions, with a more consistent C4 pattern in the older-adult cohort.
motivation: At fixed network size, Shannon graph complexity reflects entropy and dispersion of edge weights. A complementary analysis was added to assess how those weights are organized into communities.
methods: Calculate weighted Newman–Girvan modularity Q with resolution γ = 1. Keep all channels and edges touching the frontal or parietal region under study and set other edges and self-connections to zero. Apply the same regional mask across classes, without class-dependent thresholding. Compare participant-level Q between classes with paired Wilcoxon tests in the main FDR family.
results: The manuscript reports significant differences between C4 and each lower class across bands and both regions in the older-adult cohort. The young-adult cohort also showed significant class contrasts in multiple conditions.
interpretation: The data support class-dependent differences in weighted community organization. Changes in edge strengths can also alter Q, so the finding cannot isolate a change in topology from a shift in the underlying strength distribution.
conclusion: Weighted modularity adds a complementary view of community structure under a fixed regional mask.
limitations: The results depend on weights, regional masks and sensor montage. They cannot localize source-level networks or identify age-related mechanisms.
keywords: Q Newman Girvan resolution topology community edge weights older-adult cohort young-adult cohort

title: Bootstrap stability of theta connectivity
question: How stable are participant- and class-averaged theta networks when the contributing one-second epochs are resampled?
summary: Reported median Spearman correlations exceeded 0.7 for the resampling comparison of averaged networks.
motivation: One-second windows preserve stimulus timing, but contain few theta cycles. The bootstrap checks whether the averaged connection ranking is sensitive to which epochs contribute.
methods: For each participant and relative class in the older-adult cohort, average available theta-band AEC matrices to form a reference. Draw 1,000 bootstrap samples of the original epoch count with replacement, average each draw, and calculate Spearman correlation to the reference over the 120 unique edges. Summarize each participant–class combination by its median bootstrap correlation.
results: The reported median correlations exceeded 0.7. The displayed class distributions summarize stability of the rank pattern across resampled averages.
interpretation: The connection ranking in an averaged network is broadly stable under resampling from its own epoch set. The resampled matrices and reference share the same source observations.
conclusion: The bootstrap supports stability of averaged theta AEC patterns under this resampling procedure.
limitations: The analysis covers theta in the older-adult cohort. It does not estimate single-epoch accuracy or agreement with longer windows, nor was independent test–retest reliability assessed here.
keywords: theta 1 second short window AEC 1000 spearman bootstrap reliability

title: Sensitivity to ocular and muscular artifact correction
question: Do the principal Shannon complexity effects persist after additional ICA-based artifact correction?
summary: All 60 distinct class contrasts remained significant after FDR correction in each pipeline in the older-adult cohort.
motivation: Eye and muscle signals can affect EEG connectivity, especially at high frequencies. Comparing an added ICA correction with the original preprocessing quantifies the sensitivity of the main pattern to the automatically identified components.
methods: Run EEGLAB ICA on continuous 1–60 Hz EEG with a 49–51 Hz notch and common average reference in all 1,043 recordings from the older-adult cohort. Use 15 components after rank reduction. Remove components with ICLabel Eye or Muscle probability ≥ 0.80. Apply the same 4-SD epoch rejection, then repeat the successful-trial Shannon complexity analysis with the same regions, bands and participant pairing. Each pipeline’s 60 Shannon contrasts form a separate Benjamini–Hochberg family in the supplementary workbook.
results: A total of 444 components were removed across 357 recordings (34.2%). Mean rejection rates were similar, with C4 at 42.60% before and 42.85% after ICA. All 60 pairwise tests remained significant in both pipelines. For the gamma C4–C1 contrast, r changed from 0.860 to 0.853 frontally and from 0.863 to 0.869 parietally.
interpretation: The class-dependent effect persisted after removing the components identified by ICLabel, making those components alone an unlikely explanation. The counts quantify automated classifications and removals.
conclusion: The main Shannon complexity result in the older-adult cohort was robust to this additional ocular and muscular correction pipeline.
limitations: No independent electrooculogram or electromyogram recordings were available to measure residual contamination. This sensitivity analysis does not guarantee artifact-free EEG and was confined to the older-adult cohort.
keywords: EEGLAB ICLabel artifacts EOG EMG ocular muscular gamma ICA preprocessing
